None of the collection's documents describes extracting critical materials from magnets, and none describes a mixture of ethylene glycol and polyethylene glycol being used for extraction. The only magnet-related words are about separating battery materials by magnetic separation in recycling, and the only magnet-adjacent use of cobalt is as a general application.

What the documents do say about ethylene glycol (EG) is limited to battery electrode recycling. In the cssc-2020 paper, EG is used to

runs.quote: ethylene glycol was used to recover more than 90% of cobalt

runs.text:
from an LCO cathode. That is a leaching of battery cathode metals, not magnet material, and the solvent is a deep eutectic mixture, not EG with PEG.

Polyethylene glycol appears only as a component of a PANI-PEG polymer coating on cathode particles in the ensm-2021 paper, not as an extraction solvent. Magnetic separation appears only as a step in battery recycling, where

runs.quote: including sieving, magnetic separation, and density separation

runs.text:

rendered:
The documents do not answer this. None of the collection's documents describes extracting critical materials from magnets, and none describes a mixture of ethylene glycol and polyethylene glycol being used for extraction. The only magnet-related words are about separating battery materials by magnetic separation in recycling, and the only magnet-adjacent use of cobalt is as a general application.

What the documents do say about ethylene glycol (EG) is limited to battery electrode recycling. In the cssc-2020 paper, EG is used to delaminate electrode materials from current collectors, and the paper states that it is used to delaminate electrode materials at low[1] temperatures. A related review notes that a choline chloride and ethylene glycol green solvent was used in a leaching step to ethylene glycol was used to recover more than 90% of cobalt[2] from an LCO cathode. That is a leaching of battery cathode metals, not magnet material, and the solvent is a deep eutectic mixture, not EG with PEG.

Polyethylene glycol appears only as a component of a PANI-PEG polymer coating on cathode particles in the ensm-2021 paper, not as an extraction solvent. Magnetic separation appears only as a step in battery recycling, where including sieving, magnetic separation, and density separation[3] are used to remove casings and other parts from battery material.

So the answer, from these documents, is that there is no evidence that an EG and PEG mixture can extract critical materials from magnets. The closest supported fact is that EG alone has been used for battery electrode separation and in a leaching solvent for battery cathode metals.[4]
